match.reason: No point in the bank covers the resources boom; nearby points like e-govtrade, e-bop and e-ad teach the general theory, not this specific episode of China-driven commodity prices, a rising dollar and squeezed export industries.

draft.title: The resources boom
card: In the 2000s, fast growth in China raised its demand for Australian resources such as iron ore and coal. This pushed up world prices for these commodities.
Higher prices made mining more profitable, so mining investment rose sharply. Export earnings rose, and so did national income.
Strong demand for Australian dollars to pay for exports helped push the exchange rate up, so the dollar appreciated.
A higher dollar makes Australian exports dearer for overseas buyers and imports cheaper. Export industries such as manufacturing, tourism and education were squeezed as a result.
draft.remember: The boom raised mining income and the dollar, and the higher dollar hurt other exporters.

a.q: Why did the resources boom put pressure on Australia's manufacturing exporters?
opts: The higher dollar made their exports dearer overseas
Lower commodity prices cut their export earnings
Mining firms stopped buying Australian dollars
Cheaper imports made the dollar fall in value
a.why: The boom lifted the dollar, so Australian goods cost more for overseas buyers. Commodity prices rose rather than fell, so lower prices are not the cause.
a.clue: Think about what a higher dollar does to export prices.

b.q: Lena runs a winemaking business in the Barossa that sells most of its wine to Asia. During the resources boom, what was most likely to hurt her sales overseas?
opts: A rising dollar made her wine dearer for buyers abroad
Falling iron ore prices reduced demand for her wine
Higher mining investment gave her cheaper export prices
A falling dollar made her wine dearer for buyers abroad
b.why: The boom raised the dollar, so her wine cost more in foreign currency and she was squeezed. The boom did not lower the dollar, and iron ore prices were rising, not falling.
b.clue: Ask what happened to the dollar, then to the price overseas.

a.best: The higher dollar made their exports dearer overseas

b.best: A rising dollar made her wine dearer for buyers abroad
